title: Needs and wants
job: Say what you want and don't want
verifiedBy: LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: möchten is this module's verb, and it carries the level's politeness in a single word: ich möchte · Sie möchten. Ich will einen Kaffee is grammatical German and it is blunt — the shape a counter, a ticket window or a landlord wants is möchte.
Wanting to DO something is möchte plus a BARE infinitive, and the infinitive goes to the END of the clause: Ich möchte einen Kaffee trinken — "I would-like a coffee drink".
Nothing at all stands between the two verbs. English's "want TO drink" pushes a preposition into a slot German keeps empty, and Ich möchte zu trinken is that habit written out.

THE CLAUSE BRACKET, and the slogan to refuse before it is learnt: "German puts the verb at the end" is false of every sentence in this module. A German main clause is VERB-SECOND — möchte is the second element and never moves — and what goes to the end is the NON-FINITE part, here the infinitive. The two halves BRACKET the clause with the object inside them; nothing is reversed.

The accusative arrives, and it is visible on the MASCULINE ONLY: ein becomes einen in front of a masculine object. eine (feminine) and ein (neuter) look exactly as L1-M1 left them, which is precisely why the one ending that does move is the one that gets dropped.
nicht negates a verb, an adjective or a whole sentence, and it stands AFTER the verb or at the end of the clause, never in front of it: Ich trinke nicht, Der Kaffee ist nicht gut.
kein negates a NOUN — the noun that would otherwise take ein or no article at all — and it inflects exactly like ein: kein Brot (n), keine Suppe (f), keinen Kaffee (m, accusative).

English spends one word, "not", where German spends two, and the split is by TARGET rather than by emphasis or politeness. Ich möchte nicht Brot puts the verb-negator in front of a noun, which is the one place nicht cannot stand: a negated noun takes kein.

A yes/no question is still the statement with the verb moved to the front, exactly as L1-M2 taught it, and there is still no German word standing in for English "do": Möchten Sie einen Tee? The Sie form takes the plural ending -en, so it is spelled like the infinitive.

A whole class of thing, or an amount nobody is counting, takes a BARE noun: Ich möchte Wasser is "I'd like some water", with nothing at all in front of it. This is the same bare generic L1-M1 taught in Ich mag Kaffee, and it is the OPPOSITE of French and Spanish, which put the definite article there — J'aime le café, Me gusta el café.

words.note: The polite want, and a frozen form rather than a tense to learn: ich möchte · Sie möchten. It takes a thing (Ich möchte einen Kaffee) or a bare infinitive parked at the end of the clause (Ich möchte einen Kaffee trinken). Its blunt neighbour is Ich will, which is a different verb and — a warning L1-M6 will have to repeat — is not the English "will" at all. Ich mag, from L1-M1, is a standing preference and answers nothing this word asks.

ein wearing the accusative -en, in front of a masculine noun that is the object of the sentence. This is the whole visible accusative in L1: eine and ein do not move, so einen is the only ending a learner can actually see arrive. It is a different written word from L1-M1's ein, so both stay reachable, and its negative twin is keinen.

sentences.trap: English can order with nothing in front of the noun — "I'd like coffee" — and German at this counter cannot leave the ending off the article it does use. The article is not the hard part; the -n on it is.
sentences.sound: ö is the vowel of "bed" said with the lips rounded for "boot" — the mouth of one and the lips of the other. The ch after it is the soft hiss English makes at the front of "hue", never the k of "school". Kaffee is stressed on the first syllable, KAH-fay, with a long final -ee.

variations.changed: swap the thing — Tee is masculine too, so einen does not move
a feminine noun instead, and the article goes back to eine: the accusative is invisible here
the verb moves to the front for the question, and the Sie form takes the plural -en

mistake.why: Kaffee is masculine and it is the object of möchte, so its article takes the accusative -en: einen Kaffee. ein is the shape it has as a SUBJECT, which is where L1-M1 met it.

sentences.usage: At a counter, a table or a ticket window — the everyday polite order, and the shape to reach for with anyone you address as Sie.
sentences.mnemonic: One extra -n is the entire accusative in this level: einen, keinen. If the noun is masculine and it is what you want, add the n.

words.note: soup — feminine, die Suppe, so eine Suppe whether it is the subject or the object. A noun in -e is very often feminine, which is one of the endings that make German gender less arbitrary than it is usually sold as.

sentences.trap: A learner who has just met einen over-applies it, and Ich möchte einen Suppe is the result. The accusative moves the masculine article and nothing else in this level.
sentences.sound: Suppe has the short u of English "put", clipped short by the doubled p, and a final -e that is a real quiet vowel, "uh". German never leaves a written final e silent the way English does in "tape".

verb-first question, Sie form
negate the noun and eine becomes keine — kein- is ein- with a k in front of it

mistake.why: -en is the MASCULINE accusative ending. Suppe is feminine, so its article is eine in the accusative exactly as it was in the nominative: nothing moves.

sentences.usage: Ordering food, or saying what you are after in a shop or a canteen.
sentences.mnemonic: Feminine and neuter sit still. Only the masculine article walks to the accusative.

words.note: water — neuter, das Wasser. Here it stands BARE, with no article at all, because it is an unmeasured amount rather than one countable thing: Ich möchte Wasser is "I'd like some water". That is the same bare generic L1-M1 met in Ich mag Kaffee, and it is the OPPOSITE of French and Spanish, which put the definite article there.

sentences.trap: French and Spanish want a little word in front of an uncounted noun — du café, del agua — and German wants nothing. A learner arriving from either language reaches for an article German does not use here.
sentences.sound: German w is an English V: Wasser starts VA-, never WA-. The a is short and open, and the double s is a plain hiss, never the buzz English puts in "laser".

variations.changed: swap the thing — the bare noun works the same for anything uncounted

variations.cue: I would like to drink water
variations.changed: the infinitive is added at the END and the bare noun stays inside the bracket
verb to the front, and the question is asked of somebody

mistake.why: Two things at once. Wasser is neuter, so it could never take eine; and for an unmeasured amount German writes the noun with no article at all. das Wasser would be grammatical and would mean one particular water — the glass already on the table.

sentences.usage: Asking for something you do not count — water, bread, coffee by the amount rather than by the cup.
sentences.mnemonic: Uncounted means unaccompanied: no article at all.

sentences.cue: I would like to eat something
sentences.glossEn: I would like to eat something

words.note: something, anything — one word, no article, and it sits where an object sits, INSIDE the bracket the two verbs make.

essen, to eat. This one written word does three jobs and a tap on any of them lands here. It is the INFINITIVE, parked at the end of a clause after möchte. It is also the Sie FORM — Sie essen — because the plural of a regular verb is spelled exactly like the infinitive, which is what makes the Sie register cheap. And capitalised, das Essen, it is the noun "food"; L1 keeps its food concrete (Brot, Kaffee, Wasser, Suppe) so nothing here has to lean on that third reading. One warning about the ear rather than the eye: er isst ("he eats") is spelled with two s and is a DIFFERENT word from ist ("is"). They sound alike and they are never the same word.

sentences.trap: English puts "to" between the two verbs and German puts nothing, and English keeps them side by side while German pushes the second one past the object to the end of the clause. Both habits have to go at once.
sentences.sound: essen has a short, open e and a hard double s, ESS-n — the final -en collapses to a syllabic n in ordinary speech. In etwas the w is again a V, ET-vass, and the final -s is hissed, not buzzed.

variations.cue: I would like to drink something
variations.changed: swap the verb at the end — the bracket does not care which infinitive fills it

variations.cue: I would like to eat bread
variations.changed: a real object instead of etwas, still inside the bracket

variations.cue: Would you like something to eat?
variations.changed: verb-first question, and the infinitive still holds the end of the clause

mistake.why: There is no word for "to" between a modal and its infinitive. möchte takes the bare verb, and the verb goes to the end: Ich möchte etwas essen.

sentences.usage: Said to a host, a waiter or a colleague — the polite way of saying you are hungry without saying so.
sentences.mnemonic: Two verbs, one clause: the first one is second, the second one is last.

sentences.cue: I would like to drink a coffee
sentences.glossEn: I would like to drink a coffee

words.note: trinken, to drink: ich trinke · Sie trinken. As with essen, the infinitive and the Sie form are the same written word — the register decision paying for itself a second time. At the end of this clause it is the infinitive; at the front of Trinken Sie Kaffee? it would be the question.

sentences.trap: This is the sentence that kills "German puts the verb at the end". möchte is SECOND and does not move; only trinken is last. The clause is a bracket with einen Kaffee sitting inside it.
sentences.sound: The r at the start of trinken is made at the BACK of the mouth, near where you gargle, not with the tip of the tongue. The -en at the end collapses to a syllabic n: TRINK-n.

variations.cue: I would like to drink a tea
variations.changed: swap the object inside the bracket; both ends stay where they are

variations.cue: I would like to drink water
variations.changed: a bare uncounted noun in the object slot instead of an article plus a noun

variations.cue: Would you like to drink a coffee?
variations.changed: the finite verb goes first for the question and the infinitive still holds the end

mistake.why: The object goes INSIDE the bracket, not after it. English keeps its two verbs together and German does not: möchte second, einen Kaffee in the middle, trinken last.

sentences.usage: Suggesting, accepting, or saying what you are about to do — the polite shape of a plan.
sentences.mnemonic: möchte opens the bracket, the infinitive closes it, and everything you are talking about lives between them.

words.note: tea — masculine, der Tee, so einen Tee as an object, beside einen Kaffee. Two masculine drinks make the accusative ending drillable without a second grammar point.

sentences.trap: There is no German word standing in for English "do". A learner hunting for the German "do you…" is hunting for a word that does not exist: the verb simply moves to the front and nothing is inserted behind it.
sentences.sound: Tee is one long "ay", TAY, not the English "tee". In Möchten the ö returns and the -en again collapses to n: MÖCH-tn.

variations.changed: a feminine noun, so eine — the ending is invisible again

variations.cue: Would you like something to drink?
variations.changed: an infinitive at the end turns the offer into an activity
the same words as a statement: the verb drops back into second place

mistake.why: This is English's "do you…" translated word by word. tun is a real German verb and it means "to do" in its own right, but it never helps another verb the way English's does — there is nothing to insert. The question is built by moving the verb you already have: Möchten Sie einen Tee?

sentences.usage: Offering — the sentence a host, a colleague or a shop assistant says to you, and the one you say back.
sentences.mnemonic: No German "do" to find and none to add: pick the verb up and put it in front.

words.note: The negator of a NOUN, and it is ein with a k welded on the front — so it takes ein's endings and nothing else: kein Brot (neuter), keine Suppe (feminine), keinen Kaffee (masculine object). Use it wherever the positive sentence would have had ein or no article at all. It never negates a verb or an adjective; that is nicht's job, and choosing between the two by TARGET is this module's sharpest work.
bread — neuter, das Brot, so ein Brot for a loaf and kein Brot for none of it. Neuter articles never move for the accusative, so this noun shows the negation cleanly with no ending to argue about.

sentences.trap: English negates with one word in front of the verb — "I don't want bread" — and German negates the NOUN instead. Ich möchte nicht Brot is that English shape imported whole, and it is the commonest error in the module.
sentences.sound: ei is always the vowel of English "eye": kein is KINE, never "keen". That is the single most useful sound rule German has — ei says "eye", ie says "ee". Brot has a long closed o and a back-of-the-mouth r.

variations.changed: another neuter noun — kein is unchanged in front of it
a feminine noun, so keine: kein- wears ein-'s endings
the negative question, verb first — and the answer that contradicts it is L1-M2's Doch

mistake.why: nicht negates verbs, adjectives and whole sentences; it cannot stand in front of a noun. A negated noun takes kein, which is why German needs two words where English needs one.

sentences.usage: Refusing an offer, or correcting an order — polite, because möchte is still doing the asking.
sentences.mnemonic: kein for a thing, nicht for everything else. Ask what is being denied, not how strongly.

words.note: kein wearing the same accusative -en that einen wears, for the same reason: the noun behind it is masculine and it is the object. It is its own written word, distinct from kein, so both rows stay reachable — and the pair einen/keinen is the whole visible accusative of this level.

sentences.trap: The -n is easy to miss for an English ear and invisible to an English grammar, so it is dropped twice as often in the negative as in the positive. Ich möchte kein Kaffee is the same slip as Ich möchte ein Kaffee, one word later.
sentences.sound: keine is KINE-uh and keinen is KINE-en. The accusative -n is a real, audible consonant at the end of the word, and it is exactly the sound a learner leaves off.

variations.changed: another masculine noun — keinen again, for the same reason
a neuter noun, so kein loses the ending: only the masculine moves
the same negation inside a verb-first question

mistake.why: Kaffee is masculine and it is the object, so the negator takes the accusative -en: keinen Kaffee. kein Kaffee is the shape it has as a SUBJECT.

sentences.usage: Turning something down at a counter without turning the person down.
sentences.mnemonic: einen and keinen rhyme because they are the same ending on the same word, one k apart.

words.note: The feminine of kein, and it does not move for the accusative any more than eine does — keine Suppe is the same shape whether the soup is the subject or the object. It is a separate written word from kein and keinen, so it keeps its own entry and its own note.

sentences.trap: Having just learned to add -n, a learner adds it here too. The feminine has nothing to add: eine and keine are already the accusative.
sentences.sound: keine is two syllables, KINE-uh, with the quiet final -e sounded. Suppe ends the same way, so the two words rhyme and the phrase has an easy shape in the mouth.

variations.cue: I don't want to eat any soup
variations.changed: the infinitive is added at the END and the negated noun stays inside the bracket
a masculine object instead, and the -n comes back
verb-first question over the same negation

mistake.why: -en is the masculine accusative. Suppe is feminine, so its negator is keine, exactly as its article was eine.

sentences.usage: Refusing a dish — the polite refusal at a table rather than a flat no.
sentences.mnemonic: Whatever ein does, kein does. Learn one set of endings, use it twice.

words.note: The negator of a verb, an adjective or a whole sentence — never of a noun. It stands AFTER the verb it negates, and at the very end when it negates the sentence: Ich trinke nicht, Der Kaffee ist nicht gut. English's single "not" splits here into nicht and kein, and the line between them is drawn by WHAT is being denied, not by how strongly.

sentences.trap: English builds this negative out of a helper verb — "I DO not drink" — and German builds it out of nothing at all. There is no German "do" to find, so there is none to negate: the verb stays where it is and nicht follows it.
sentences.sound: The ch in nicht is the soft hiss of English "hue", made with the tongue high and forward; it never becomes a k. trinke ends in the quiet -e, TRINK-uh.

variations.changed: swap the verb — nicht still follows it
nicht in front of an ADJECTIVE instead, which is its other target

variations.cue: I don't want to drink any coffee
variations.changed: the noun is what is denied here, so kein- does it and nicht stays away

mistake.why: nicht never stands in front of the verb it negates. The finite verb keeps second position and nicht comes after it: Ich trinke nicht.

sentences.usage: Declining on principle rather than on this occasion — the standing "I don't".
sentences.mnemonic: No German "do", so nothing to put "not" in front of. It goes behind the verb instead.
